sources.note: Nothing. Ch.2 Phonology (pp.23-29) covers consonants, vowels, phonotactics and clusters only; no stress/accent section or statement. Only incidental uses of 'unstressed' (ba 'and' is 'an unstressed function word', p.23; locative -a 'could be simply an unstressed -n heard as -a', ch.3) and a remark (p.28) that apparent initial clusters (krip~karip 'thigh', mrat 'ground', truwal 'man') are probably first-vowel reduction 'as in English suppose'. The work is a consolidation of 19th-c. written sources, which did not mark accent.

sources.note: Nothing. Stewart's 'Structure of the Tongue' (pp.125-127) treats number, case, pronouns, tenses, numerals; the vocabulary has only notes like '(pronounced short)' on a few monosyllables. No word on accent.

sources.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian languages: a late survey. Pacific Linguistics B-77. Canberra: ANU. p.233, 'Two phrases from the Buŋandidj language (Mt Gambier)'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement; only data. The only modern phonetic record of the language: two phrases remembered by an old woman whose father came from Mt Gambier, transcribed with Hercus's tonic-stress mark on the first syllable of every word: beŋid wilidj [ˈbɛ·ŋɪt ˈwilɪtj] 'no sleep'; diḏman luen [ˈdɪṯmʌn ˈlu·ən] 'I am hungry'. Four disyllables, all initial-stressed; Hercus makes no comment on Bunganditj accent.

sources.citation: Mathews, R.H. 1903. Language of the Bungandity Tribe, South Australia. Journal and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New South Wales 37: 59-74.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on word accent. 'Orthography' (pp.63-64) describes letters and sounds only. The sole use of 'accentuation' is sentence-level: 'An interrogative sentence does not differ in form from an assertive one, the distinction being indicated by the tone and accentuation of the speaker's voice' (p.61).
